# Matplotlib {background-color="#03A062"}

## Figures, axes and artists

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{python}
t = np.linspace(0, 10, 200)
env = np.exp(-t / 3)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4.5, 2.6))
ax.plot(t, env * np.sin(2 * t),
        label="signal")
ax.plot(t, env, "--", label="envelope")
ax.set_xlabel("time (s)")
ax.set_title("One Figure, one Axes")
ax.legend();
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
* **Figure**: the whole canvas, saved to a file
* **Axes**: one plot area; a figure can hold many
* **Artists**: everything drawn (lines, text, ticks), each with properties you can change
:::
::::

## `pyplot` versus `fig, ax`

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**pyplot style**: acts on the "current" axes

```python
plt.plot(x, y)
plt.xlabel("time (s)")
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Object-oriented style**: says which axes

```python
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(x, y)
ax.set_xlabel("time (s)")
```
:::
::::

<br>

* We use `fig, ax` throughout: it scales to many panels and works inside functions
* Most `plt.xlabel(...)` calls become `ax.set_xlabel(...)`

::: {.source-note}
Matplotlib docs, [the two interfaces](https://matplotlib.org/stable/users/explain/figure/api_interfaces.html).
:::

## Saving figures

```python
fig.savefig("figure.pdf")                                # vector: line plots, for papers
fig.savefig("figure.png", dpi=300, bbox_inches="tight")  # raster: images, slides
```

* The extension picks the format
* `bbox_inches="tight"` trims the white border

## Live coding: a first figure {.live-coding}

* Plot a damped oscillation with the defaults
* Improve it: size, colours, line styles, limits, labels, legend
* Save it as PNG and PDF
* The same plot in `pyplot` style, for comparison

::: {.notes}
```python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

t = np.linspace(0, 10, 500)
signal = np.exp(-t / 3) * np.sin(2 * np.pi * t)

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(t, signal)                           # defaults

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3))
ax.plot(t, signal, color="black", linewidth=1, label="signal")
ax.plot(t, np.exp(-t / 3), "--", color="tab:orange", label="envelope")
ax.set_xlim(0, 8)
ax.set_xlabel("time (s)")
ax.set_ylabel("amplitude")
ax.set_title("A damped oscillation")
ax.legend(loc="upper right")

fig.savefig("damped.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")
fig.savefig("damped.pdf")

plt.plot(t, signal)                          # pyplot style
plt.xlabel("time (s)")
```
:::

## More plot types

| Method | For |
|---|---|
| `ax.scatter(x, y, s=..., c=...)` | Points, with size and colour per point |
| `ax.hist(values, bins=...)` | Distributions |
| `ax.bar(names, heights)` | Values per category |
| `ax.errorbar(x, y, yerr=...)` | Means with error bars |
| `ax.imshow(array)` | Images and 2-D arrays |

* Several panels: `fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3)`, then `axes[0].plot(...)`

## Images and colormaps

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{python}
moon = plt.imread("data/moonlanding.png")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2,
                         figsize=(5, 2))
axes[0].imshow(moon)
axes[1].imshow(moon, cmap="gray")
for ax in axes:
    ax.set_axis_off()
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
* A 2-D grey image has no colour: `imshow` maps values through a **colormap**
* Perceptually uniform maps (`viridis`, `gray`); diverging maps (`RdBu_r`) only for data centred on zero
* `fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax)` shows the mapping
:::
::::

## Live coding: panels and images {.live-coding}

* Reaction times: a histogram and a scatter plot side by side
* Colour points by a second variable
* Show an image with a colormap and a colorbar
* Crop with slicing, then show the crop

::: {.notes}
```python
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
rt = rng.normal(450, 120, size=200)
correct = rng.random(200) < 0.8

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 3))
axes[0].hist(rt, bins=20)
axes[0].set_xlabel("reaction time (ms)")
axes[1].scatter(np.arange(200), rt, c=correct, s=10, cmap="coolwarm")
axes[1].set_xlabel("trial")
axes[1].set_ylabel("reaction time (ms)")

moon = plt.imread("data/moonlanding.png")
moon.shape, moon.dtype

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
im = ax.imshow(moon, cmap="gray")
fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax)

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.imshow(moon[100:250, 50:300], cmap="magma")   # a crop, another colormap
```
:::

## When to reach for seaborn

* **seaborn:** a tidy DataFrame; colour, size or panels by category; means with confidence intervals; distributions
* **Plain Matplotlib:** arrays and images, custom layouts, unusual plot types
* seaborn draws **with** Matplotlib: `ax=`, `fig.savefig` and the last block still apply

# SciPy {background-color="#03A062"}

## What lives where

| Submodule | For |
|---|---|
| `scipy.optimize` | Fitting (`curve_fit`), minimising, root finding |
| `scipy.stats` | Distributions, statistical tests |
| `scipy.signal` | Filtering, spectra, peak finding |
| `scipy.fft` | Fourier transforms |
| `scipy.ndimage` | N-D image filters, morphology, measurements |

* `import scipy as sp`, then `sp.optimize.curve_fit`, `sp.stats.ttest_ind`, ...
* Also `interpolate`, `integrate`, `linalg`, `sparse`, `spatial`

## Fitting a model

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{python}
import scipy as sp

def model(t, amplitude, rate):
    return amplitude * np.exp(-rate * t)

t = np.linspace(0, 5, 40)
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
noise = rng.normal(0, 0.1, t.size)
y = model(t, 3.0, 1.2) + noise

params, cov = sp.optimize.curve_fit(
    model, t, y, p0=[1, 1]
)
errors = np.sqrt(np.diag(cov))
params.round(2), errors.round(2)
```
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
* The model's first argument is `x`; the rest are the parameters to fit
* `p0`: a starting guess
* Standard errors: the square root of the covariance's diagonal
:::
::::

## Fourier transforms

* Any signal is a sum of waves of different frequencies
* The **spectrum** shows how much of each frequency there is
* Periodic noise shows up as isolated peaks
    * Remove them, then transform back
* `sp.fft` has the forward and inverse transforms, in 1-D, 2-D and N-D

## Live coding: removing mains hum {.live-coding}

* A slow 3 Hz signal plus 50 Hz hum and noise
* Its spectrum: where is the hum?
* Zero the hum, transform back, compare

::: {.notes}
```python
import scipy as sp

fs = 500                                     # samples per second
t = np.arange(0, 2, 1 / fs)
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
clean = np.sin(2 * np.pi * 3 * t)
recorded = clean + 0.8 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 50 * t) + rng.normal(0, 0.2, t.size)

spectrum = sp.fft.rfft(recorded)
freqs = sp.fft.rfftfreq(t.size, d=1 / fs)
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(freqs, np.abs(spectrum))
ax.set_xlabel("frequency (Hz)")             # peaks at 3 and 50

spectrum[np.abs(freqs - 50) < 2] = 0        # a mask on the frequencies
filtered = sp.fft.irfft(spectrum, n=t.size)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3))
ax.plot(t, recorded, alpha=0.4, label="recorded")
ax.plot(t, filtered, label="hum removed")
ax.legend()
```
:::

# scikit-image {background-color="#03A062"}

## Images are NumPy arrays

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
```{python}
import skimage as ski

rgb = ski.data.hubble_deep_field()
image = ski.color.rgb2gray(rgb)
print(rgb.shape, rgb.dtype)
print(image.shape, image.dtype)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(3, 3))
ax.imshow(image, cmap="gray")
ax.set_axis_off()
```
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
* Grey `(rows, cols)`; colour `(rows, cols, 3)`; stacks add `z` or time
* Usually `uint8` or `uint16`; most filters return `float` in [0, 1]
* Everything from NumPy works: slicing crops, masks select
* Today we count **galaxies**; in the exercise you count **nuclei**
:::
::::

## Filtering and thresholding

```{python}
smoothed = ski.filters.gaussian(image, sigma=2)   # reduce noise
threshold = ski.filters.threshold_yen(smoothed)   # automatic threshold
binary = smoothed > threshold                     # a boolean mask

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(9, 3))
images = {"original": image, "gaussian": smoothed, "Yen": binary}
for ax, (title, im) in zip(axes, images.items()):
    ax.imshow(im[:250, :250], cmap="gray")
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.set_axis_off()
```

* Several rules pick the threshold: Otsu, Li, Yen, triangle, ...; each gives a different mask

## Live coding: looking and thresholding {.live-coding}

* Load the Hubble image: shape, dtype, colour to grey
* Its histogram: what is sky, what is galaxy?
* Smooth with different `sigma`
* Compare two thresholds

::: {.notes}
```python
import skimage as ski

rgb = ski.data.hubble_deep_field()
rgb.shape, rgb.dtype
image = ski.color.rgb2gray(rgb)
image.shape, image.dtype, image.min(), image.max()

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.hist(image.ravel(), bins=100, log=True)   # mostly dark sky

crop = image[:250, :250]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(10, 3))
for ax, sigma in zip(axes, [0.5, 2, 5]):
    ax.imshow(ski.filters.gaussian(crop, sigma=sigma), cmap="gray")
    ax.set_title(f"sigma={sigma}")

smoothed = ski.filters.gaussian(image, sigma=2)
t_yen = ski.filters.threshold_yen(smoothed)
t_li = ski.filters.threshold_li(smoothed)
t_yen, t_li

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8, 4))
axes[0].imshow(smoothed > t_yen, cmap="gray")
axes[1].imshow(smoothed > t_li, cmap="gray")
(smoothed > t_yen).mean(), (smoothed > t_li).mean()   # fraction marked as galaxy
```
:::

## Labelling and segmentation

```{python}
cleaned = ski.morphology.remove_small_objects(binary, max_size=20)
cleaned = ski.segmentation.clear_border(cleaned)
labels = ski.measure.label(cleaned)  # 0 = background, 1..N = objects
print("objects found:", labels.max())

overlay = ski.color.label2rgb(labels, image=image, bg_label=0)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 2.2))
ax.imshow(overlay[300:520, :])
ax.set_axis_off()
```

* Touching objects merge into one; a **watershed** separates them (stretch exercise)

## Measuring objects with `regionprops`

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="62%"}
```{python}
props = ski.measure.regionprops_table(
    labels,
    intensity_image=image,
    properties=["label", "area",
                "eccentricity", "intensity_mean"],
)
galaxies = pd.DataFrame(props)
galaxies.head(4).round(2)
```
:::
::: {.column width="38%"}
* One row per object, ready for pandas and seaborn
* Dozens of properties: `perimeter`, `centroid`, `bbox`, `intensity_*`, ...
* Measured in **pixels**: multiply by the pixel size for µm
:::
::::

## Live coding: label and measure {.live-coding}

* Remove specks and objects on the border
* Label, count, and overlay the labels on the image
* Measure every galaxy into a DataFrame
* Which galaxies are the most elongated? Is size related to brightness?

::: {.notes}
```python
binary = smoothed > t_yen
cleaned = ski.morphology.remove_small_objects(binary, max_size=20)
ski.measure.label(cleaned).max()             # count before clearing the border
cleaned = ski.segmentation.clear_border(cleaned)
labels = ski.measure.label(cleaned)
labels.max()

overlay = ski.color.label2rgb(labels, image=image, bg_label=0)
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.imshow(overlay)

props = ski.measure.regionprops_table(
    labels, intensity_image=image,
    properties=["label", "area", "eccentricity", "intensity_mean", "centroid"],
)
galaxies = pd.DataFrame(props)
galaxies.describe()
galaxies.sort_values("eccentricity").tail()  # the most elongated

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.scatter(galaxies["area"], galaxies["intensity_mean"], c=galaxies["eccentricity"])
ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_xlabel("area (pixels)")
ax.set_ylabel("mean brightness")
```
:::

# Whirlwind tour {background-color="#03A062"}

## xarray: labelled N-D arrays

* **Problem:** with NumPy you must remember that time is axis 0
* Dimensions have **names**; coordinates have **values** (seconds, channel numbers, µm, brain areas)
* Select by label, reduce by name, group by a coordinate

```python
lfp.sel(time=slice(622.5, 624), channel=200)
lfp.mean(dim="time")
lfp.groupby("area").mean()
```

::: {.source-note}
[tutorial.xarray.dev](https://tutorial.xarray.dev)
:::

## Live coding: a labelled recording {.live-coding}

* Wrap the LFP in a `DataArray`: `time` and `channel`, plus `area` and `depth` per channel
* Select by session time and by brain area, not by position
* Reduce over `time`; group by `depth` and by `area`
* Spike counts with three named dimensions, grouped by stimulus strength

::: {.notes}
Follow the Demo section of `day2_05_xarray.ipynb`.

```python
lfp = xr.DataArray(raw * uV_per_count, dims=("time", "channel"),
                   coords={"time": lfp_start + np.arange(raw.shape[0]) / sampling_rate,
                           "channel": np.arange(raw.shape[1]),
                           "area": ("channel", area), "depth": ("channel", depth_um)})

lfp.sel(channel=200).sel(time=slice(stim_on[89] - 0.5, stim_on[89] + 1)).plot()
lfp.sel(channel=lfp.area == "SSp-n")
lfp.std(dim="time").plot(y="depth")
lfp.groupby("depth").mean().plot(x="time", y="depth", cmap="RdBu_r", robust=True)

rate = counts.mean("unit").groupby("strength").mean() / 0.05
rate.plot.line(x="time", hue="strength")
```
:::

## dask: bigger than memory, in parallel

* A dask array is a grid of NumPy **chunks**
* Operations are **lazy**: they only build a task graph
* `.compute()` runs the graph on all cores, a few chunks at a time
* `xr.open_dataset(..., chunks={...})` makes xarray use dask

::: {.source-note}
[tutorial.dask.org](https://tutorial.dask.org)
:::

## Live coding: 10 minutes of LFP {.live-coding}

* A 4.6 GB stand-in for 10 minutes of raw-rate LFP, 1.5 million samples × 384 channels
* NumPy-style operations return instantly
* `.compute()` runs them; check the answer
* Read an HDF5 file lazily with `da.from_array`: the same code would run on the 51 GB original

::: {.notes}
Follow the Demo section of `day2_06_dask.ipynb`.

```python
import dask.array as da

x = da.random.normal(0, 100, size=(1_500_000, 384), chunks=(25_000, 384))
x                                   # the chunk diagram

channel_std = (x - x.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True)).std(axis=0)
channel_std                         # instant: just a graph
len(channel_std.__dask_graph__())

%time channel_std.compute().mean()  # just under 100

with h5py.File("data/ibl_session.h5") as f:
    lazy = da.from_array(f["lfp/data"], chunks=(1000, 384))
    lazy.std(axis=0).compute()
```
:::

## napari: look at your data

* An interactive viewer for N-D images and annotations: labels, points, shapes, tracks
* Sliders for z, time and channels
* Each layer's `.data` is a NumPy array you can read back
* Opens a **desktop window**: run it on your own laptop

::: {.source-note}
[napari.org/stable/tutorials](https://napari.org/stable/tutorials/)
:::

| **scikit-learn** | Machine learning: classification, clustering, regression ([SPL chapter](https://lectures.scientific-python.org/packages/scikit-learn/index.html)) |
| **Zarr** | Chunked, compressed N-D arrays on disk or in the cloud |
| **Polars** | Fast DataFrames with a lazy query engine |
| **Numba** | Compiles Python loops to machine code with `@numba.njit` |

## Wrap-up

* **Plot** with `fig, ax = plt.subplots()`; seaborn for tidy DataFrames
* **Check SciPy** (and scikit-image) before writing an algorithm yourself
* **Images are arrays**: filter, threshold, label, then measure into a DataFrame
* **Scale up** with xarray (labels), dask (size) and napari (looking)

**Keep going:** the [Scientific Python Development Guide](https://learn.scientific-python.org/development/), the advanced chapters of Scientific Python Lectures [@spl], and the [BioImage Analysis Notebooks](https://haesleinhuepf.github.io/BioImageAnalysisNotebooks/).
